text: {"master_id": "jody-fisher", "work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "diatonic-tonic-or-subdominant-I-or-IV", "narrative": "Fisher prescribes using the major scale for improvisation over Maj7 chords, noting that harmonizing any major scale produces two Maj7 chords (I and IV), giving the player two parent-scale choices. The example given in Chapter 4 (p. 56) is CMaj7 as part of the diatonic progression CMaj7-Amin7-FMaj7-G7, over which 'you could improvise over this with the C Major scale because all of these chords are natural to the key of C.'", "source_principle_ids": ["jody-fisher:jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning:major-scale-harmony-system:scale-choice-per-chord-quality", "jody-fisher:jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning:major-scale-harmony-system:mode-to-chord-correspondence"], "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning", "references": [{"source": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning", "citation": "chapter 5 p. 77"}, {"source": "jazz-guitar-method-vol-1-beginning", "citation": "chapter 4 p. 56"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "diatonic-tonic-voiced-with-retained-third-and-seventh", "narrative": "Fisher prescribes retaining the 3rd and 7th in any Maj7 voicing. This means that we combine the root, 3rd, 5th and 7th degrees of the major scale to build the chord. Notice that what we have actually done is add the 7th degree to a major triad.'
